Check before you post:

  • UK words go in the title. Alternatives go in fields or tags where the platform allows, once each.
  • Never use a word that would make a UK buyer expect something different.
  • Save the table in your notes app and reuse it for every listing in that category.

Keywords checklist

Next: Module 05 for photos, then Module 06 to price the item from sold listings you look up yourself.

05 Photos

Buyers cannot pick your item up. Your photos are the closest they get, so they do most of the describing before anyone reads a word.

AI cannot take your photos for you, but it is very good at three jobs:

  1. Planning the shots so you do not forget the label, the flaw or the back.
  2. Checking your photo set against your Listing Brief, so the pictures and the words agree.
  3. Writing captions and alt text quickly.

Every prompt here starts from your Listing Brief (see module 01). Keep it open in your notes app and paste it in where the prompt says.

The one rule about edited and AI photos

Your photos must show the actual item you are sending, in its actual condition.

  • Cropping, straightening and a little brightness are normal and fine.
  • Removing a stain, a scratch or bobbling with an editing tool is not fine. Nor is changing the colour, adding a background that suggests something is included when it is not, or using an AI-generated "model" image that makes the item look different from the real one.
  • Stock photos and photos copied from other listings or brand websites are not fine for second-hand items. They show someone else's item, not yours.

Platforms take this seriously, and rules differ:

PlatformWhat their rules say, in short
eBay UKPhotos must accurately represent the item. Stock photos are not allowed for used, damaged or defective items. No added borders, text or watermarks. You are responsible for content you create with AI tools.
VintedUse your own photos showing the item's current condition. No stock, watermarked or found-online images, no collages. Show the whole item first, show labels on branded items, and show any defects. Vinted's catalogue rules also say photos must show the item as it is, without editing.
EtsyListings must accurately represent what the buyer will receive. Etsy has specific rules on AI-assisted items and how to disclose AI use.
TikTok Shop UKRealistic AI images or video must be labelled, and AI must not make the product look different from reality (texture, features, size). No text or watermarks other than product branding.
Depop, Amazon UKBoth require images that accurately show the product. Amazon has strict main image rules (for example a pure white background and only what is included).

Rules change. Check the current rule in the platform's help pages before you use any AI editing or background tool. If in doubt, leave it out.

A misleading photo is also a fast route to an "item not as described" claim, which you will usually lose.

Quick reference: shot lists by category

Use this as a starting point. Prompt PH1 tailors it to your exact item.

CategoryMust-have shotsNice to have
ClothingFront flat or on hanger, back, brand label, size label, care or material label, every flaw close upDetail of buttons, zips, fabric texture, lining, measurements with tape
Shoes and bootsPair side on, both soles, inside (insole and size), heel backs, toe caps, every scuffBox if included, laces, top-down view
ElectronicsFront, back, all ports, serial or model label, screen switched on, every scratch, everything included laid outBattery health screen, test in use, original box
HomewareWhole item, underside with any maker's mark, every chip or crack, scale (next to a common object)In a plain room setting, detail of pattern
Books and mediaFront cover, spine, back cover, copyright page (for edition), any marks, disc surface for CDs and DVDsPage edges, inscription, dust jacket close up
Toys and collectablesWhole item, all parts laid out, box all sides, any maker's mark, every mark or missing partBatteries compartment, working lights or sound in a short video
HandmadeWhole piece, detail of finish, scale, back or underside, every colour option you sellPackaging, the piece in use

PH1 Shot list for my item

Use it when: you have written the Listing Brief and want a numbered shot list before you pick up your phone. Paste this:

You are an experienced UK marketplace seller helping me plan listing photos.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

I am listing on: [PLATFORM]
Most photos this platform allows (check the app): [NUMBER OR "NOT SURE"]

Write a numbered shot list for this exact item. For each shot give:
1. What to photograph.
2. The angle or distance.
3. Why a buyer needs it (one short line).

Rules:
- Use UK English.
- Base the list only on facts in my brief. If a shot depends on something the brief does not say (for example whether there is a box or a size label), write [CHECK: ...] instead of assuming.
- Put the main (cover) photo first, then the back, then labels, then every flaw listed in my brief, then details.
- Give every flaw in my brief its own shot.
- If I have more shots than the platform allows, mark which ones to combine or drop, and never drop a flaw shot.
- No filters, no editing that changes colour or hides wear. Say so at the end.
- Keep it short enough to read on a phone.

What good output looks like:

Item: Clarks black leather Chelsea boots, UK 6, light creasing across toes, small scuff on left heel.

  1. Cover: pair side on, left boot in front, plain floor, phone at boot height. Shows shape and colour.
  2. Front: both toes towards camera. Shows the toe creasing honestly.
  3. Back: both heels. Shows heel wear and pull tabs.
  4. Soles: both soles side by side, top down. Buyers judge wear from the soles.
  5. Inside: size and brand stamp on insole. Proves size and brand.
  6. Flaw: left heel scuff, close up, with a coin next to it for scale.
  7. Flaw: toe creasing, close up, in daylight.
  8. Detail: elastic side panel, stretched slightly. Shows it has not gone baggy. [CHECK: is the elastic still firm?]

[CHECK: is there a box? If yes, add one shot of it.] No filters or editing that changes colour or hides wear.

Check before you post:

  • Every flaw in your brief has its own photo.
  • The cover photo shows the whole item, not a close up.
  • Any [CHECK] notes are answered before you shoot.

PH2 Flaw photo checklist

Use it when: your item has any wear, marks or faults and you want to show them properly (this protects you as much as the buyer). Paste this:

Help me photograph the flaws on my item honestly and clearly.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Anything else I have noticed since writing the brief:
[EXTRA FLAWS, OR "NONE"]

Do the following:
1. List every flaw mentioned above as a checklist.
2. For each flaw, tell me how to photograph it so it is clearly visible: distance, angle, lighting, and what to put next to it for scale (a coin, a ruler or a tape measure).
3. Suggest a short caption for each flaw photo that matches the wording in my brief exactly.
4. List common places flaws hide on this type of item that my brief does not mention, as questions for me to check (for example "Have you checked the armpits for bobbling?"). Label these [CHECK: ...]. Do not assume they are flawed.

Rules: UK English. Do not describe any flaw as smaller or less noticeable than my brief says. No reassuring words like "barely noticeable" unless my brief uses them. Plain, factual wording only.

What good output looks like:

Item: grey Next wool-blend jumper, size 12, small bobbling under arms.

Flaw checklist

How to shoot it: lay the jumper flat, lift one arm out to the side, shoot from about 20 cm in daylight from a window. Side light shows bobbling better than light from straight on. Put a ruler along the bobbled patch.

Caption: "Small bobbling under both arms, shown close up."

Also worth checking:

  • [CHECK: any bobbling on the sides or front where a bag strap would rub?]
  • [CHECK: cuffs stretched or marked?]
  • [CHECK: any small holes? Hold it up to a window.]
  • [CHECK: any smell, such as smoke or perfume? Mention it in the description if so.]

Check before you post:

  • The flaw is visible at phone screen size, not just when zoomed in.
  • Captions use the same words as your description.
  • Anything new you find goes into your Listing Brief too.

PH3 Phone lighting and background plan

Use it when: you are photographing at home with just a phone and want better, more accurate colour without buying kit. Paste this:

I photograph listings on my phone at home. Help me set up for this item.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

My set-up:
- Phone: [PHONE MODEL, OR "NOT SURE"]
- Time I usually shoot: [E.G. WEEKDAY EVENINGS]
- Space I have: [E.G. SMALL BEDROOM, WINDOW FACING NORTH]
- Things I own that could be a background: [E.G. WHITE DUVET COVER, GREY WALL, WOODEN FLOOR]

Give me:
1. The best place and time to shoot, using the window light I have.
2. Which of my backgrounds suits this item's colour and why.
3. Five phone camera tips in plain English (focus, exposure, lens cleaning, avoiding zoom, avoiding flash glare).
4. How to check the colour in the photo matches the real item before I post.
5. What to do if I must shoot after dark, using only ordinary household lamps.

Rules: UK English, no jargon, short numbered steps. Do not recommend buying anything. Do not suggest any editing that changes the item's colour or hides wear.

What good output looks like:

Item: mustard yellow cotton cardigan, size M.

  1. Where and when: shoot near your north-facing window in daylight, ideally at the weekend. North light is soft and even, which suits a strong colour like mustard.
  2. Background: the grey wall. White can make mustard look darker than it is, and wood will clash.
  3. Tips: wipe the lens on your top first. Tap the screen on the cardigan to focus. Slide the brightness down slightly if the colour looks washed out. Step closer rather than zooming. Flash off.
  4. Colour check: hold the cardigan next to your phone screen in the same light. If the photo looks more orange or paler, retake it rather than editing the colour.
  5. After dark: turn off the main ceiling light, use two lamps either side at the same height, and say "photographed in lamplight, colour may look slightly warmer" only if it genuinely does.

Check before you post:

  • The colour on screen matches the item in daylight.
  • Nothing in the background could be mistaken as included.

PH4 Photo set audit

Use it when: you have taken your photos and want a second pair of eyes to spot gaps before you post. Paste this:

Check my photo set against my Listing Brief before I post.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Here is a plain description of each photo I have taken, in order:
1. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 1, E.G. "FRONT OF JUMPER, FLAT ON BED"]
2. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 2]
3. [ADD MORE LINES AS NEEDED]

(If your AI tool accepts images, you can upload the photos instead. Only upload photos of the item, never anything showing addresses, faces or personal documents.)

Tell me:
1. Missing shots: anything a buyer would expect for this item that is not in my set.
2. Mismatches: anything in the photos that contradicts the brief (for example a flaw shown but not in the brief, or an item in shot that is not included in the sale).
3. Order: the best order for these photos, with the cover photo first.
4. Privacy: anything in the background I should crop out (post, family photos, house number, reflections).

Rules: UK English. Only comment on what I have described or shown. If you cannot tell something, write [CHECK: ...]. Be direct and brief.

What good output looks like:

Item: Tefal 1.7 litre kettle, white, limescale inside, small chip on lid.

Missing: a photo of the base plate and plug, and one of the inside showing the limescale (it is in your brief, so show it). Mismatch: photo 3 shows two mugs next to the kettle. Buyers may think they are included. Retake without them or say clearly they are not included. Order: 1 (front), 4 (lid chip close up moved up), 2 (back), then base. Privacy: photo 2 shows a letter on the worktop. Crop it out or retake. [CHECK: does the kettle still boil? If yes, a short video of it boiling helps.]

Check before you post:

  • Nothing in any photo suggests something is included when it is not.
  • No post, faces, number plates or house numbers anywhere in the frame (including reflections in shiny items).

PH5 Photo captions

Use it when: your platform lets you add a caption or short text to each photo, or you want matching lines to use in the description. Paste this:

Write one short caption for each of my listing photos.

Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

My photos, in order:
1. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 1]
2. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 2]
3. [ADD MORE AS NEEDED]

Rules:
- UK English, 12 words or fewer per caption.
- Plain and factual. Say what the photo shows, not how great it is.
- Flaw captions must use the same wording as my brief and must not play the flaw down.
- Only use facts from the brief. If a caption needs a fact I have not given, write [CHECK: ...].
- No hype words (stunning, gorgeous, must-have, rare), no emojis, no exclamation marks.

What good output looks like:

Item: Le Creuset 20 cm cast iron casserole, Volcanic orange, light marks on enamel inside.

  1. Front view, 20 cm casserole in Volcanic orange.
  2. Lid on, handles both sides shown.
  3. Inside: light marks on the enamel, see close up.
  4. Close up of marks on the base of the inside.
  5. Underside with size stamp. [CHECK: what number is stamped?]
  6. Next to a 1 litre milk bottle for scale.

Check before you post:

  • Captions match the description word for word on flaws.
  • Nothing says "rare", "vintage" or "authentic" unless you can back it up.

PH6 Alt text for listing photos

Use it when: your platform or your own shop has an alt text box (a short written description of an image for people using screen readers). Etsy and most web shops have one. Paste this:

Write alt text for each of my product photos.

Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Photos, in order:
1. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 1]
2. [DESCRIBE PHOTO 2]
3. [ADD MORE AS NEEDED]

Character limit for alt text on my platform (check the help pages): [NUMBER OR "NOT SURE"]

Rules:
- UK English. Describe what is in the image plainly, as if to someone who cannot see it: item, colour, angle, and any flaw shown.
- Do not start with "Image of" or "Photo of".
- Do not stuff keywords or repeat the title. Alt text is for people, not search.
- Only use facts from my brief. If you need a detail I have not given (such as the exact colour), write [CHECK: ...].
- If I have not given a limit, keep each one under 125 characters.

What good output looks like:

Item: handmade blue ceramic mug, speckled glaze, 350 ml.

  1. Speckled blue ceramic mug with a curved handle, side view on a wooden table.
  2. Top view inside the mug showing the pale blue glaze and darker speckles.
  3. Unglazed base with a stamped maker's mark. [CHECK: what does the mark say?]
  4. Mug held in a hand to show size, roughly the height of a palm.

Check before you post:

  • Each line describes the photo, not the sales pitch.
  • No list of search terms tacked on the end.

PH7 Is this edit OK?

Use it when: you are tempted to use a background remover, a "magic eraser", an AI model or any AI photo tool, and want to check it will not misrepresent the item. Paste this:

I want to edit a listing photo. Tell me whether the edit risks misrepresenting my item.

Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
The original photo shows: [DESCRIBE THE ORIGINAL]
The edit I want to make: [E.G. REPLACE MESSY BEDROOM BACKGROUND WITH PLAIN WHITE / REMOVE A HAIR / PUT JUMPER ON AI MODEL]
The tool I would use: [TOOL NAME OR TYPE]

Answer in three parts:
1. **Risk:** low, medium or high that the edit changes how the item looks (colour, condition, size, shape, what is included). Explain in one or two lines.
2. **Safer option:** a way to get a similar result without editing the item itself (for example reshooting on a plain sheet).
3. **Platform rule:** remind me that I must check the current photo and AI rules in the [PLATFORM] help pages. Do not state specific rules as fact unless I have pasted them in below.

Platform rule text I have copied from the help pages (optional):
[PASTE RULE TEXT, OR "NONE"]

Rules: UK English. Be honest, not reassuring. If the edit would hide or reduce any flaw in my brief, say plainly that I should not do it.

What good output looks like:

Item: cream Zara linen shirt, size S, faint mark on left cuff. Edit: remove background and use an AI model wearing the shirt.

  1. Risk: high. An AI model image generates a new version of the shirt. The fit, colour and creases may change, and the cuff mark may disappear. That misrepresents the actual item.
  2. Safer option: hang the shirt on a door against a plain wall, shoot in daylight, and include the cuff close up. If you want to show fit, give chest and length measurements.
  3. Platform rule: check the current photo and AI rules in Vinted's help pages before using any editing tool. If you post edited images, the real flaws must still be clearly visible in your own unedited photos.

Check before you post:

  • At least one unedited photo of the real item is in the set.
  • Every flaw from your brief is still visible after any edit.
  • You have checked the platform's current photo rules.

PH8 Choose my cover photo

Use it when: you have several decent shots and want to pick the first one buyers see in search. Paste this:

Help me choose the cover (first) photo for my listing.

Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
My candidate photos:
A. [DESCRIBE PHOTO A]
B. [DESCRIBE PHOTO B]
C. [DESCRIBE PHOTO C]

Pick one and explain why in two lines. Judge on: the whole item is visible, colour looks true, background is plain, the item fills most of the frame, and it would still be clear as a small square thumbnail on a phone.
Then say what one change would make the winning photo better when I reshoot.

Rules: UK English. Do not suggest adding text, borders, stickers or badges to the photo (many platforms do not allow them). Do not suggest hiding flaws in the cover photo by angle alone if the flaw is major; say so if it is.

What good output looks like:

Item: Lego Creator 3 in 1 set, built, box included, one missing minifigure.

Pick: B (built model on a plain white sheet, front on). The whole model is visible and it reads clearly as a thumbnail. A has the box cut off, and C is too dark. One change: step back slightly so there is a small gap around the model on all sides, as square crops can cut the edges. The missing minifigure is a major point, so show it in photo 2 and put it in the first line of the description.

Check before you post:

  • The cover photo shows the item you are selling, not a box or a stock image.
  • Major flaws are shown early in the photo set, not hidden at the end.

06 Pricing

Pricing is where most sellers guess. These prompts replace the guess with a quick, written reason you can stand behind.

We are honest about what they do: they help you set a sensible price from real evidence and do the sums properly. They cannot promise a sale, a profit or a particular price. Buyers decide that.

The rule: you find the sold prices, the AI does the maths

AI chat tools do not know what your item sold for last week. If you ask "what is this worth?" with nothing else, you get a confident guess. Do not use it.

Instead:

  1. Look up sold listings yourself on the platform you are selling on. On eBay, search for your item and turn on the "Sold items" filter. On other apps, look for items marked as sold, and remember that an asking price is not a sold price.
  2. Copy the details of 5 to 10 comparable items into your notes app: title, sold price, postage, condition, and the date if you can see it. Matching items are better than lots of items.
  3. Paste them into the prompt along with your Listing Brief.

Please do not use scraping tools, bots or browser add-ons that harvest listings automatically. Most platforms' terms forbid it, and you do not need it. Ten minutes of looking gives you better comps anyway, because you can see which items actually match yours.

What makes a good comp

Good compWeak comp
Same brand, model or style"Similar" items from a different brand
Same or similar sizeDifferent size (especially children's clothes and shoes)
Similar conditionNew with tags against your well-worn item
Sold in the last few monthsSold two years ago
Sold price with postage notedAsking price on an unsold listing

R1 Tidy my sold comps

Use it when: you have copied a messy pile of sold listings into your notes and want them in a clean table before pricing. Paste this:

I have copied some sold listings I found myself. Put them into a clean table so I can compare them with my item.

My Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Sold listings I copied (paste exactly as copied, messy is fine):
[PASTE YOUR SOLD LISTINGS HERE]

Make a table with these columns: Title (shortened), Sold price £, Postage £ (or "free" or [CHECK]), Total paid £, Condition, Size or model, Date sold (or [CHECK]), Match to my item (Good, Partial, Poor) and a one-line reason.

Rules:
- UK English, prices in pounds.
- Only use numbers that appear in what I pasted. Never invent a price, date or condition. If a detail is missing, write [CHECK].
- If something looks like an asking price rather than a sold price, flag it with [CHECK: sold or asking?].
- Put Good matches first.
- Below the table, list any comps I should drop and why, in one line each.

What good output looks like:

Item: grey Next wool-blend jumper, size 12, small bobbling under arms.

TitleSold £Postage £Total £ConditionSizeDateMatch
Next grey wool blend jumper12.002.9914.99Good123 weeks agoGood: same style and size
Next grey crew neck knit10.50free10.50Good14[CHECK]Partial: one size up
Next wool mix jumper grey NWT22.003.2025.20New with tags121 month agoPoor: new, yours is worn

Drop: the NWT one. New with tags is not comparable with a worn jumper with bobbling.

(Example figures only, invented for illustration.)

Check before you post:

  • Every price in the table is one you actually saw.
  • You have at least three Good matches before moving on to R2.

R2 Price from my sold comps

Use it when: you have your tidied comps and want a list price, a realistic range and a floor. Paste this:

Suggest a price for my item using only the sold listings I have found.

My Listing Brief (includes my price floor, the lowest I will accept):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
Do buyers pay postage on top, or is it included in my price? [ON TOP / INCLUDED]
My sold comps (ideally the table from R1):
[PASTE COMPS HERE]

Give me:
1. The sold price range from the Good matches only (lowest to highest), and the middle (median) value.
2. How my item compares: better, same or worse condition than the Good matches, based only on my brief.
3. A suggested list price, a likely accepted price, and my floor from the brief. If my floor is above what the comps support, say so plainly.
4. Two or three lines of reasoning I could save in my notes.

Rules:
- UK English, pounds, show your working in simple sums.
- Use only the numbers I pasted. Do not use outside knowledge of prices.
- If I have fewer than three Good matches, say the evidence is thin and tell me what to search for.
- Do not promise the item will sell, or at what price. Say "based on these comps" not "this will sell for".
- Write ranges as "£10 to £14", never with a dash.

What good output looks like:

Item: Clarks black leather Chelsea boots, UK 6, light toe creasing, small heel scuff. Floor £18.

  1. Good matches sold for £20 to £32. Median £25.
  2. Your condition: similar to most Good matches. The heel scuff puts you slightly below the two best ones.
  3. List at £28, expect offers around £22 to £25, floor £18. Your floor sits comfortably below the range.
  4. Reasoning: five Good matches, median £25. Listing a little above median leaves room for offers. Scuff disclosed, so no surprises for the buyer.

Based on these comps only. Buyers set the final price.

Check before you post:

  • The range comes only from your pasted comps.
  • Your floor still covers fees and postage (use R7 to check).

R3 Adjust for condition and extras

Use it when: your item is not quite like the comps (better or worse condition, missing box, extra accessories) and you want a fair adjustment. Paste this:

My item is different from the comps I found. Help me adjust the price fairly.

My Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

My closest sold comps:
[PASTE COMPS HERE]

How my item differs from these comps (in my own words):
[E.G. "NO ORIGINAL BOX, BUT COMES WITH A SPARE CHARGER" / "MINE HAS A SMALL CHIP, THEIRS DID NOT"]

Do the following:
1. List each difference and whether it pushes the price up, down or makes no clear difference, with a one-line reason a buyer would recognise.
2. If the comps themselves show the effect (for example boxed sold higher than unboxed), use those numbers and show the sum. If they do not, say "the comps do not show this" and give a cautious suggestion, clearly labelled as a judgement, not evidence.
3. Give an adjusted list price and floor.

Rules: UK English, pounds. Only use numbers I have pasted. Never guess a "collector's value". Do not tell me to describe the item as better than my brief says.

What good output looks like:

Item: Nintendo Switch Lite, turquoise, working, light scratches on screen, no box, includes case.

  1. No box: down. In your comps, boxed ones sold at £95 and £100, unboxed at £82 and £85. Roughly £12 to £15 less.
  2. Light screen scratches: down. Your comps do not show this clearly. Judgement: buyers are cautious with screens, so price towards the lower end of unboxed.
  3. Includes case: small plus, but the comps do not show a clear difference.

Adjusted list price £85, floor £75.

(Example figures only, invented for illustration.)

Check before you post:

  • Differences are in your description too (no box, scratches, extras).
  • Judgement calls are labelled as judgement in your own notes.

R4 Bundle pricing

Use it when: you want to sell several items together, or a buyer asks for a bundle price. Paste this:

Help me price a bundle.

Items in the bundle (one short Listing Brief or line each, with my individual list price and floor):
[PASTE ITEMS HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
Postage for the bundle as one parcel: £[AMOUNT OR "NOT SURE"]
Postage if sent separately (total): £[AMOUNT OR "NOT SURE"]
Does the platform have its own bundle discount tool I have switched on? [YES, WITH % / NO / NOT SURE]

Give me:
1. The total of individual list prices and the total of floors.
2. The postage saving from sending one parcel (if I gave both figures).
3. A suggested bundle price and the lowest bundle price I should accept, keeping every item at or above its floor in total.
4. A one-line reason I can send the buyer, based on the postage saving and my time, without pressure.

Rules: UK English, pounds, show the sums. Use only my numbers. If postage is missing, write [CHECK: postage] and do the sum without it. Do not use pressure wording such as "today only" or "last chance".

What good output looks like:

Bundle: three children's Frugi tops age 4 to 5 (£8, £8, £7 list; £6, £6, £5 floor).

  1. List total £23. Floor total £17.
  2. Postage saving: £3.20 as one parcel against £8.40 separately, so £5.20 saved.
  3. Suggested bundle price £19, accept down to £17.
  4. Line to send: "I can do all three for £19. They go in one parcel, so it saves on postage for both of us."

(Example figures only, invented for illustration.)

Check before you post:

  • The bundle price is at or above the total of your floors.
  • If the platform applies its own bundle discount on top, you have included it in your sums.

R5 Offer strategy

Use it when: you want to decide in advance what offers to accept, counter or decline, so you are not deciding at 11pm with a lowballer waiting. Paste this:

Help me set an offer plan for this listing.

My Listing Brief (includes my floor):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
My list price: £[AMOUNT]
My reasoning from comps (optional, e.g. from R2): [PASTE OR "NONE"]
Does the platform let me set automatic accept or decline levels? [YES / NO / NOT SURE]

Give me a simple plan:
1. Accept straight away at or above: £...
2. Counter-offer if between: £... and £..., with the counter price I should send.
3. Politely decline below: £...
4. If auto accept or decline is available, the levels I could set (and a reminder to check the settings in the app).
5. One short, polite line for each case that I could send.

Rules: UK English, pounds. Never go below my floor. Do not suggest fake scarcity or pressure ("someone else is interested", "ends tonight") unless I tell you it is true. Keep replies friendly and brief.

What good output looks like:

Item: Le Creuset 20 cm casserole, list £65, floor £48.

  1. Accept at £58 or more.
  2. Counter offers from £48 to £57 at £56.
  3. Decline below £48.
  4. Auto settings: accept £58, decline under £45 (a little below your floor so you still see near misses). Check how your app's offer settings work.
  5. Lines:
    • Accept: "Thanks, happy to accept. It will be posted within [CHECK: dispatch time]."
    • Counter: "Thanks for the offer. The lowest I can do is £56, as it is heavy to post."
    • Decline: "Thanks, but that is too low for me. You are welcome to make another offer."

Check before you post:

  • Every figure is at or above your floor.
  • Any reason you give (like heavy postage) is true.

R6 Planned price drop schedule

Use it when: an item has not sold and you want a calm plan for reducing it, rather than panic-dropping or leaving it forever. Paste this:

Make a price drop plan for an item that has not sold yet.

My Listing Brief (includes my floor):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Platform: [PLATFORM]
Current price: £[AMOUNT]
Listed for: [NUMBER] days
Views, likes or watchers so far (if the app shows them): [NUMBERS OR "NOT SURE"]
My sold comps (optional): [PASTE OR "NONE"]

Give me:
1. First, a quick check of things other than price that could be holding it back (cover photo, title, missing measurements, postage cost). Base this only on my brief, and write [CHECK: ...] for anything you cannot see.
2. A drop plan with dates in weeks from today, the price at each step, and the point where I stop at my floor.
3. What to do if it still has not sold at the floor (bundle it, relist fresh with new photos, sell elsewhere, donate).

Rules: UK English, pounds. Never go below my floor. Keep drops simple (round numbers). Do not tell me any step will make it sell. If my platform lets me send offers to people who liked or watched the item, mention it as an option to check in the app, not as a guarantee.

What good output looks like:

Item: cream Zara linen shirt, size S, listed 21 days at £14, 40 views, 2 likes, floor £8.

  1. Check first: your brief has no chest measurement [CHECK: add pit to pit and length]. Linen creases, so check the cover photo is not crumpled.
  2. Plan:
    • Week 1: fix measurements and cover photo, keep at £14.
    • Week 2: £12. Consider sending an offer to the two likers if the app allows it.
    • Week 4: £10.
    • Week 6: £8 (floor). Stop here.
  3. If still unsold: bundle it with other size S linen, relist with fresh photos in spring, or donate.

Check before you post:

  • The plan stops at your floor.
  • You fix any listing problems before dropping the price.

R7 Fee and postage maths

Use it when: you want to know what you actually keep after fees, postage and packaging, before you set a price or accept an offer. Paste this:

Work out what I keep from a sale. I will give you the current fees myself.

Platform: [PLATFORM]
Sale price: £[AMOUNT]
Postage the buyer pays: £[AMOUNT OR "NONE, INCLUDED IN PRICE"]
My actual postage cost: £[AMOUNT]
Packaging cost: £[AMOUNT OR "0"]
Fees I copied from the platform's current fee page today (paste exactly, e.g. percentage, fixed fee per order, whether it applies to postage too, payment processing):
[PASTE CURRENT FEE DETAILS HERE]
What I paid for the item (optional): £[AMOUNT OR "NOT SURE"]

Show me, as a simple table:
1. Money in (sale plus postage paid by buyer).
2. Each fee, with the sum shown.
3. Postage and packaging out.
4. What I keep.
5. If I gave a cost price: what is left after that cost.
Then tell me the lowest sale price at which I would still keep £[TARGET AMOUNT] after costs, using the same fees.

Rules:
- UK English, pounds, round to the nearest penny.
- Use ONLY the fee details I pasted. Do not use fees from your own knowledge, they may be out of date. If my fee details are unclear, write [CHECK: ...] and explain what is unclear.
- This is a sum, not advice. Do not call the result "profit" unless I gave a cost price, and do not promise any outcome.
- Remind me that fees and rules change, so I should check the platform's current fee page each time.

What good output looks like:

Item: Tefal kettle. Sale £15, buyer pays £3.50 postage, actual postage £3.20, packaging £0.30. Fees pasted by the seller (invented for this example): 10% of total including postage, plus £0.30 per order.

Fixed fee0.30

You keep18.50 minus 5.6512.85

To keep at least £10 with these fees, the lowest sale price is about £11.84 [shown working: (10 + 0.30 + 3.20 + 0.30) divided by 0.9, minus 3.50]. Fees and rules change: check the platform's current fee page before relying on this.

(The fee figures above are invented to show the maths. They are not any platform's real fees.)

Check before you post:

  • You pasted today's fees from the platform's own help pages.
  • You weighed the parcel and checked the real postage price.
  • You noted whether you sell as a private seller or a business, as fees can differ (check the current fee page).

R8 Is it worth listing on its own?

Use it when: you have a low-value item and are not sure whether to list it alone, bundle it, or let it go. Paste this:

Help me decide whether this item is worth listing on its own.

My Listing Brief:

Compare four options in a short table: list alone, bundle with similar items, list as part of a job lot, or donate or recycle. For each, give: effort, likely money kept (only from my numbers, otherwise [CHECK]), and one line on when it makes sense.
Then give a one-line recommendation.

What good output looks like:

Item: paperback thriller, good condition. Comps £2 to £3 sold. You keep about £0.60 after postage. 15 minutes per item.

(Example figures only, invented for illustration.)

  • Job lot photos show everything included.

07 Buyer messages

Messages eat evenings. "Is this still available?", the £3 offer on a £20 coat, the parcel stuck in a depot, the return request you are not sure you have to accept.

These prompts help you reply quickly, politely and correctly. They are built on three rules:

  1. Be polite, brief and factual. You are writing for the buyer and, if it ever gets that far, for the platform's support team reading the thread later.
  2. Stay on the platform. Every message and every payment goes through the app.
  3. Respect the buyer's rights. Never refuse a legal right or a platform protection, and never pressure anyone about feedback.

This module is practical guidance, not legal advice. If a dispute is serious, check the platform's help pages, gov.uk or Citizens Advice.

Privacy: never paste the buyer's personal details into the AI

When you paste a buyer's message into an AI tool, remove their name, username, address, phone number, email and order number first. Replace them with [BUYER] or [ORDER]. The AI does not need them to write a good reply, and you should not be sharing someone else's personal data with a third-party tool. Paste your reply back into the app and add the name there if you want to.

Also remove anything personal about you, such as your home address or surname.

Never move payment off the platform

If a buyer asks to pay by bank transfer, PayPal "friends and family", cash on collection arranged by message, or to "message me on WhatsApp", the answer is no.

  • It removes the buyer's protection and yours.
  • It is how many scams start.
  • eBay's rules, for example, do not allow offers to buy or sell outside eBay, or sharing contact details before a sale is completed. Other platforms have similar rules. Check the current rule in the platform's help pages.

Use the platform's own offer, bundle or private offer tools instead. Template 12 below gives you a ready reply.

Returns: private sellers and traders are different

This is the part most sellers get wrong, in both directions. Here is the short version. Check the current details on gov.uk or Citizens Advice.

First, which are you? If you are clearing out your own things, you are usually a private seller. If you buy items to resell for profit, or make items to sell, you are likely to be a trader (a business) in law, even if you use a personal account. The platform's reporting to HMRC is a separate question from this. If you are not sure, read the guidance on gov.uk.

Private sellerTrader (business seller)
Item must match your descriptionYesYes
Item must be of satisfactory quality and fit for purposeNot in the same way. The main rule is "as described", so describe faults honestlyYes, under the Consumer Rights Act 2015
Buyer can reject a faulty item for a refundOnly if it was not as describedYes, generally within 30 days (the "short-term right to reject")
Buyer can cancel an online order for any reasonNo legal right to do thisYes, generally 14 days from the day after delivery, then 14 more days to send it back (Consumer Contracts Regulations 2013). Some exceptions, such as personalised items
Refund timing on cancellationNot applicableGenerally within 14 days of getting the item back or proof it was sent, including the original standard delivery charge
Can "no returns" in the listing stop this?It stops change-of-mind returnsNo. A trader cannot remove these legal rights

Platform protection sits on top of the law. Even as a private seller with "no returns", platform buyer protection can still apply:

  • eBay UK: the eBay Money Back Guarantee lets buyers ask for a refund if an item does not arrive, is faulty or damaged, or does not match the listing, even when the seller does not accept returns. Buyers generally have 30 days from delivery.
  • Vinted Pro: Vinted is for private second-hand selling, and traders are expected to use Vinted Pro. Vinted's Pro terms require Pro sellers to accept returns within 14 days of receipt.
  • Vinted: buyers have a short window after Vinted says the parcel should have arrived (2 days at the time of writing) to report an issue under Buyer Protection. If they do not, the order completes.
  • Depop, Etsy, Amazon UK and TikTok Shop UK each have their own buyer protection and returns rules.

Rules and time limits change. Check the current rule in the platform's help pages before you reply to any return or refund request.

The practical upshot: an honest listing with every flaw described and photographed is your best protection. If it was as described, you are on firm ground. If it was not, the fair and usually required thing is to sort it out.

M1 Reply to any buyer message

Use it when: you have a message that does not fit the other prompts, or you just want a quick, polite reply. Paste this:

Help me reply to a buyer on [PLATFORM]. I have removed their name and personal details.

My Listing Brief (for facts about the item):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

I sell as a: [PRIVATE SELLER / BUSINESS]
Buyer's message:
[PASTE MESSAGE, WITH NAMES AND DETAILS REPLACED BY [BUYER]]

What I want to say in my own words (rough is fine):
[E.G. "YES I CAN POST TOMORROW BUT NOT BEFORE"]

Write one reply.

Rules:
- UK English, friendly and brief (under 60 words unless the situation needs more). No emojis unless I ask.
- Only state facts from my brief or my notes. If the buyer asks something I have not answered, write [CHECK: ...] instead of guessing.
- Keep everything on the platform. Never suggest paying, messaging or meeting off the platform.
- Do not promise delivery dates I have not given.
- Do not refuse any legal right or platform protection. If the message is about returns, refunds or a problem with the item, say so and suggest I use the specific prompt for it.
- Do not mention feedback or reviews.

What good output looks like:

Buyer: "Hi, does this come from a smoke free home? And can you post Saturday?" Seller notes: yes smoke free, I post Mondays and Thursdays.

"Hi, thanks for asking. Yes, it comes from a smoke-free home. I post on Mondays and Thursdays, so if you buy before Monday it will go out then. [CHECK: pet-free too? Add if true.]"

Check before you post:

  • Names, addresses and order numbers were removed before pasting.
  • Every fact in the reply is true.

M2 "Is this still available?"

Use it when: you get the classic question, and want a reply that answers it and gently moves things along. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] has asked if my item is still available. Write a short, friendly reply.

My Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

Is it still available? [YES / NO, SOLD / ON HOLD FOR SOMEONE ELSE]
When I can post: [E.G. "NEXT WORKING DAY"]
Anything useful to add: [E.G. "HAPPY TO SEND MORE PHOTOS" / "NONE"]

Rules:
- UK English, under 40 words, one clear sentence answering the question first.
- If available, add one useful fact (posting time or one key detail from the brief) and an easy next step using the platform's tools (buy now, make an offer).
- No pressure or fake urgency ("lots of interest", "going fast") unless I have told you it is true.
- Only use facts from my brief.

What good output looks like:

"Hi, yes it is still available. It is a UK 6 and I can post the next working day after purchase. Happy to send extra photos if useful."

Check before you post:

  • The item really is still available on every platform you cross-list on.
  • No urgency you cannot back up.

M3 Lowball offer

Use it when: someone offers far below your price and you want to stay polite without giving the item away. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] has made an offer much lower than my price. Help me reply.

My Listing Brief (includes my floor):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]

My list price: £[AMOUNT]
Their offer: £[AMOUNT]
What I want to do: [COUNTER AT £... / DECLINE POLITELY / ASK WHAT THEY HAD IN MIND]
Any true reason that supports my price (optional): [E.G. "SOLD COMPS AROUND £25", "HEAVY TO POST"]

Write two versions: one friendly counter-offer and one polite decline. Each under 50 words.

Rules:
- UK English, warm and calm. Never sarcastic, never lecture the buyer about value.
- Never go below my floor.
- Only give reasons I have supplied. Do not invent other buyers or deadlines.
- Suggest using the platform's offer button for any counter, so the deal stays on the platform.

What good output looks like:

Item: Le Creuset casserole, list £65, floor £48, offer £20.

Counter: "Thanks for the offer. £20 is a bit too low for me, as similar ones have sold for more. I could do £55 if that helps, and I will send it through the offer button."

Decline: "Thanks for your interest, but I cannot go that low on this one. You are welcome to make another offer."

Check before you post:

  • The counter is above your floor.
  • Your stated reason is true (you actually looked at comps).

M4 Bundle request

Use it when: a buyer wants several of your items and asks for a deal. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] wants to buy several of my items together. Help me reply with a bundle price.

The items (title, list price and floor for each):
[PASTE ITEMS HERE]

How the platform handles bundles: [E.G. "BUYER ADDS ITEMS TO A BUNDLE AND I SEND AN OFFER" / "NOT SURE"]

2. Gives the bundle price and says whether postage is included.

Rules: UK English, friendly. Keep it on the platform. Never go below the total of my floors. If the platform process is "NOT SURE", write [CHECK: how bundles work on this app] rather than guessing.

What good output looks like:

"Hi, happy to do all three Frugi tops (stripe, dinosaur and navy) for £19 plus postage, all in one parcel. If you add them to a bundle, I will send you an offer for that price."

M5 Postage questions

Use it when: a buyer asks about postage cost, speed, tracking, collection or sending abroad. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] has asked about postage. Help me reply.

- If the buyer asks for collection, only offer it if I said yes, and keep payment on the platform.
- Do not suggest undervaluing, mislabelling or marking anything as a gift on customs forms.

"Hi, I post with Tracked 48 as standard, and I can post the next working day after purchase. I cannot promise Friday delivery, sorry. [CHECK: can you offer a faster service, and at what cost?]"

  • No promised delivery date.
  • Any upgrade cost is added through the platform, not paid separately.

M6 Delay: late dispatch or parcel stuck in transit

Use it when: you are going to post late, or the tracking has stalled and the buyer is asking where their parcel is. Paste this:

Help me update a buyer on [PLATFORM] about a delay.

Type of delay: [I WILL POST LATE / PARCEL STUCK IN TRANSIT / TRACKING SAYS DELIVERED BUT BUYER HAS NOT GOT IT]
Facts:
- Date of sale: [DATE]
- Date posted (if posted): [DATE OR "NOT YET"]
- Service and whether tracked: [E.G. "TRACKED 48, YES"]
- What tracking shows now: [PASTE STATUS, NO TRACKING NUMBER NEEDED]
- What I can do next: [E.G. "POST TOMORROW MORNING" / "OPEN A CARRIER ENQUIRY"]
Buyer's message (personal details removed): [PASTE OR "NONE, I AM MESSAGING FIRST"]

Write a reply under 80 words that:
1. Says sorry once, plainly, without over-explaining.
2. Gives the facts (what has happened, what I am doing next and when).
3. Tells the buyer they are still covered by the platform's buyer protection, without quoting specific time limits.

Rules: UK English. Do not blame the buyer. Do not promise a delivery date. Do not suggest cancelling outside the platform or refunding by another method. If a fact is missing, write [CHECK: ...].

What good output looks like:

Situation: Tracked 48 posted Monday, tracking has not updated since Tuesday at a depot.

"Hi, sorry for the wait. I posted it on Monday with Tracked 48 and the tracking shows it at a depot since Tuesday. I have asked the carrier to look into it and will update you as soon as I hear. Your purchase is still covered by the platform's buyer protection in the meantime."

Check before you post:

  • Dates are correct.
  • If you have promised to follow up, set a reminder on your phone.

M7 Return request

Use it when: a buyer asks to return an item, for any reason. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] has asked to return an item. Help me work out my position and reply.

I sell as a: [PRIVATE SELLER / TRADER (BUSINESS)]
My listing's return policy: [E.G. "NO RETURNS" / "30 DAY RETURNS, BUYER PAYS POSTAGE"]
Platform return or buyer protection rules I have checked today (paste from help pages, or "NOT CHECKED"):
[PASTE RULE TEXT]
My Listing Brief (what I described):
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF HERE]
Date delivered: [DATE]
Buyer's reason (personal details removed):
[PASTE MESSAGE]

Do two things.

Part 1, my position (short bullet points):
- Is the reason change of mind, or a claim that the item is faulty, damaged or not as described?
- If I am a trader: remind me that UK buyers generally have a 14-day right to cancel most online purchases, plus the short-term right to reject faulty goods, and that "no returns" cannot remove these. Flag any exceptions only as [CHECK: ...].
- If I am a private seller: explain that change-of-mind returns are up to me and my listing policy, but claims of "not as described", faulty or damaged may be covered by platform buyer protection whatever my policy says.
- Base anything about platform rules only on the text I pasted. If I pasted nothing, tell me to check the platform's help pages before replying.

Part 2, a reply to the buyer (under 80 words): polite, clear on next steps, and using the platform's own return or refund process.

Rules: UK English. This is not legal advice, say so in one line at the end of Part 1. Never tell the buyer they have no rights. Never suggest refunding off the platform. Do not argue about the buyer's reason in the reply.

What good output looks like:

Situation: private seller, no returns, Vinted. Buyer: "It is lovely but doesn't fit, can I send it back?"

Part 1

  • This is change of mind, not a fault or "not as described".
  • As a private seller, accepting a change-of-mind return is your choice.
  • If the buyer had said the item was not as described, Buyer Protection could apply, so check the listing matched.
  • Not legal advice. Check Vinted's current help pages.

Part 2 "Hi, sorry it did not fit. As I sell privately I do not usually accept returns for fit, which is why I listed the measurements. You might find it resells well on here. Thanks for understanding."

Check before you post:

  • You are clear whether you are a private seller or a trader.
  • You checked the platform's current return and protection rules.
  • If the claim is about a fault or description, use M8 instead.

M8 "Item not as described"

Use it when: a buyer says the item is different from the listing, faulty, or has a flaw you did not mention. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] says my item is not as described. Help me respond fairly.

I sell as a: [PRIVATE SELLER / TRADER]
My original listing text (title and description):
[PASTE LISTING TEXT]
What my photos showed: [DESCRIBE, E.G. "FLAW ON LEFT CUFF SHOWN IN PHOTO 4"]
Buyer's complaint (personal details removed), and any photos they describe:
[PASTE MESSAGE]
Platform rules I have checked today (optional): [PASTE OR "NOT CHECKED"]

Do three things:
1. Compare the complaint with my listing, point by point, and say honestly whether the listing covered it, did not cover it, or it is unclear. Do not take my side automatically.
2. Suggest fair options: ask for photos, return for a full refund through the platform, a partial refund through the platform if the buyer wants to keep it, or let the platform decide. Say which fits best.
3. Write a calm reply under 90 words.

Rules: UK English. If the listing did not mention the problem, say so plainly. Never accuse the buyer of lying, even if I suspect it; if I suspect a swapped or damaged return, tell me to keep records and use the platform's process. Never refund or pay outside the platform. Never ask the buyer to change or remove feedback as part of any deal. Not legal advice.

What good output looks like:

Item: grey Next jumper. Listing said "small bobbling under arms". Buyer says "there is a hole on the back".

  1. Bobbling: covered in the listing and photos. Hole on the back: not mentioned anywhere. This is likely a fair claim unless the hole was made after delivery, which you cannot know.
  2. Best fit: offer a return for a full refund through the platform, or a partial refund if they would rather keep it.
  1. "Hi, I am sorry about that. I did not spot a hole when I listed it, so thank you for letting me know. I am happy to accept a return for a full refund through the app, or offer a partial refund if you would prefer to keep it. Just let me know which suits."

Check before you post:

  • You reread your own listing before replying.
  • Any refund goes through the platform so both of you stay covered.
  • Add a note to your checklist so the same flaw does not get missed again.

M9 Damaged in the post

Use it when: the buyer says the item arrived broken, crushed or wet. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] says the item arrived damaged. Help me handle it.

Item and how I packed it: [E.G. "GLASS VASE, BUBBLE WRAP, DOUBLE-WALLED BOX"]
Postage service: [E.G. "PLATFORM LABEL" / "MY OWN TRACKED SERVICE, COMPENSATION UP TO £..."]
Buyer's message and what they say their photos show (personal details removed):
[PASTE MESSAGE]
Platform rules I have checked today (optional): [PASTE OR "NOT CHECKED"]

Give me:
1. A short checklist of what to ask the buyer for (photos of the item, the packaging and the label) and what to keep myself (proof of postage, photos of packing if I took any).
2. Who is likely to handle the claim: the platform (for example if I used a platform label) or me with the carrier. Base this on what I told you, and if unsure write [CHECK: ...] and tell me to check the platform's help pages.
3. A calm reply to the buyer under 80 words that asks for photos and explains the next step through the platform.

Rules: UK English. Do not blame the buyer or the carrier in the reply. Do not refuse a refund in the reply. Do not suggest settling off the platform. Not legal advice.

What good output looks like:

Item: Denby stoneware mug set, bubble wrap, single-wall box, own Tracked 48.

  1. Ask the buyer for: photos of the mugs, the outer box (all sides) and the inner wrapping. Keep: proof of postage and tracking.
  2. Claim: you used your own service, so you would usually claim from the carrier yourself while the platform handles the buyer's refund request. [CHECK: the carrier's claim rules and time limit.]
  3. "Hi, I am really sorry it arrived damaged. Could you send photos of the mugs and of the box and packaging, including the outside? That helps me sort it out with the carrier. I will make sure it is put right through the app."

Check before you post:

  • Buyer photos are requested through the platform's messages, not by email.
  • You check the carrier's claim time limit today, not next week.
  • Next time: double-walled box and more padding for ceramics.

M10 Asking for feedback, without pressure

Use it when: a sale has gone smoothly and you want to send a thank-you that mentions feedback, fairly. Paste this:

Write a short thank-you message to a buyer on [PLATFORM] after delivery.

Item: [SHORT NAME]
Anything nice and true to mention: [E.G. "HOPE IT FITS WELL" / "NONE"]
Should the message mention feedback? [YES, ONE NEUTRAL LINE / NO]

Rules:
- UK English, under 40 words, warm and simple.
- If feedback is mentioned, one neutral line only, such as inviting them to leave feedback if they have a moment. Never ask for "positive" or "5 star" feedback.
- Never offer or hint at any discount, refund, freebie or reward in exchange for feedback or a review. That is against platform rules (eBay's feedback policy, for example) and UK law on fake and incentivised reviews.
- Never ask the buyer to contact me first "before leaving feedback" in a way that suggests they should not leave honest feedback.
- No emojis unless I ask.

What good output looks like:

"Hi, thanks for buying the Clarks boots. I hope they fit well. If you have a moment, feedback is always appreciated. Any questions, just message me here."

Check before you post:

  • No reward, discount or favour is linked to feedback.
  • It is sent once, not repeatedly.

M11 Difficult or abusive buyer

Use it when: a buyer is rude, threatening, demanding things not in the listing, or threatening bad feedback to get a discount. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] is being difficult. Help me respond calmly and protect myself.

What has happened (personal details removed):
[DESCRIBE OR PASTE MESSAGES]
What the listing actually said about the relevant point: [PASTE OR "NOT RELEVANT"]
Has a sale happened? [YES / NO]

Give me:
1. A one-line read of the situation: is this a genuine problem said rudely, a demand for something not in the listing, a threat linked to feedback, or abuse?
2. What to do: reply, reply once then stop, or do not reply. Include using the platform's report and block tools where relevant, and keeping all messages on the platform as a record.
3. If a reply is sensible, one calm reply under 60 words.

Rules:
- UK English. Calm, neutral, never sarcastic. Never insult or threaten the buyer back.
- If the buyer has a genuine complaint about the item, the reply must still offer the platform's proper route (return or refund process). Do not refuse legal rights because the buyer is rude.
- If the buyer is threatening negative feedback to get something not in the listing, tell me that platforms generally treat this as not allowed (eBay calls it feedback extortion) and to report it through the platform. Do not tell me to give in to it.
- If there are threats to my safety, tell me to stop replying, report it to the platform, and contact the police if I feel at risk.
- Never suggest sharing personal details or moving off the platform.

What good output looks like:

Situation: after delivery, buyer says "Refund me £10 or I'll leave negative feedback". Item was as described.

  1. Read: a threat linked to feedback, to get something not in the listing.
  2. Do: reply once, then report it through the platform's tools. Keep everything in the app's messages.
  3. "Hi, I am sorry you are not happy. The item was sent as described and photographed. If there is a problem with it, please open a request through the app and it will be looked at properly."

Check before you post:

  • You have not said anything you would mind the platform's support team reading.
  • Screenshots or messages are kept in the app in case of a dispute.

M12 Suspicious request or off-platform payment

Use it when: a buyer asks to pay another way, wants your email or phone number, asks you to post to a different address, or something just feels off. Paste this:

A buyer on [PLATFORM] has sent a request that may be risky. Help me spot the risk and reply.

The request (personal details removed):
[PASTE MESSAGE]

Give me:
1. A plain list of warning signs in the message (for example: paying outside the app, a link to click, "my courier will collect", asking for my email or phone, posting to a different address from the one in the order, overpaying and asking for money back).
2. What to do: reply, decline, report through the platform, or ignore.
3. A short, polite reply that keeps everything on the platform.

Rules: UK English. Do not help me arrange payment, contact or delivery outside the platform. Do not tell me to click any link in the message. Remind me that platform protection generally only covers sales paid for through the platform, and to check the platform's help pages on scams.

What good output looks like:

Message: "Can I pay you by bank transfer so we avoid fees? Send me your number."

  1. Warning signs: paying outside the app, asking for your phone number before a sale.
  2. Do: decline politely. Report if they push.
  3. "Hi, thanks, but I only sell through the app so we are both covered. You are welcome to buy or make an offer here."

Check before you post:

  • You have not shared any contact details.
  • You have not clicked any link sent by the buyer.

Ready-to-adapt reply templates

Short replies for everyday messages. Copy, fill in the [SQUARE BRACKETS], and check every fact is true for your item before sending. They are written to work on any platform.

1. Still available

Hi, yes it is still available. I can post [WHEN] after purchase. Any questions, just ask.

2. Sold already

Hi, sorry, this one has sold. I have a few similar items listed if you would like a look.

3. More photos

Hi, of course. I have added [WHAT] to the listing photos. Let me know if you need anything else.

4. Measurements

Hi, measured flat: pit to pit [X] cm, length [X] cm, sleeve [X] cm. I have added these to the description too.

5. Friendly counter-offer

Thanks for the offer. The lowest I can do is £[AMOUNT]. I will send it through the offer button if that works for you.

6. Polite decline

Thanks for your interest, but I cannot go that low on this one. You are welcome to make another offer.

7. Bundle price

Happy to do [ITEMS] together for £[AMOUNT] [PLUS / INCLUDING] postage, all in one parcel. If you add them to a bundle I will send you an offer.

8. Postage timing

I post [DAYS / NEXT WORKING DAY] with [SERVICE]. It usually takes [TIME] after that, but I cannot guarantee a delivery date.

9. Posted

Hi, your parcel went out today with [SERVICE]. Tracking is in the app. Thanks again.

10. Late dispatch

Hi, I am sorry, I cannot post until [DAY] because [SHORT TRUE REASON]. It will go out then and I will update you here.

11. Parcel delayed in transit

Hi, sorry for the wait. The tracking shows it at [STATUS] since [DAY]. I have asked the carrier to check and will update you as soon as I hear. You are still covered by the app's buyer protection.

12. Payment off the platform

Hi, thanks, but I only sell and take payment through the app, so we are both protected. You are welcome to buy or make an offer here.

13. Change-of-mind return (private seller, no returns)

Hi, sorry it did not suit. As a private seller I do not usually take returns for [FIT / CHANGE OF MIND], which is why I listed [MEASUREMENTS / DETAILS]. Thanks for understanding.

14. Return accepted

Hi, no problem. Please start the return in the app and I will refund you through it once it is back with me. Thanks for letting me know.

15. Item not as described

Hi, I am sorry about that, and thanks for telling me. Could you send a photo of the [PROBLEM] here? I will sort it out through the app.

16. Damaged in the post

Hi, I am really sorry it arrived damaged. Could you send photos of the item and the packaging, including the outside of the box? I will put it right through the app.

17. Thank you (with neutral feedback line)

Hi, thanks for buying the [ITEM]. I hope you enjoy it. If you have a moment, feedback is always appreciated.

18. Rude message, first reply

Hi, I am sorry you are not happy. If there is a problem with the item, please open a request through the app and it will be looked at properly.

19. Cross-listed item sold elsewhere

Hi, I am really sorry, this has just sold on another app and I have removed it. I have cancelled the order through the app so you will be refunded in full.

Template 19 applies only if an order has come in on a second platform. Cancel it through the platform's own process and check its rules, as some platforms count seller cancellations against you.

08 Video and TikTok Shop

Short videos sell things. You do not need to show your face, use your voice or film your home to make them. Everything in this module works with hands-only shots, a plain background, on-screen text and a text-to-speech voice.

This module covers two jobs:

  1. Faceless product videos for items you are selling yourself (on TikTok, Instagram, or as the video slot on a listing where the platform allows it).
  2. TikTok Shop UK copy: product titles, descriptions, a claims check, and a run-sheet for live selling.

As always, start with your Listing Brief (see module 01). The AI is only as accurate as the facts you give it.

Before you start: three rules for video

  • Show the real item. Film the exact item (or, for new stock, the exact product) the buyer will receive. No stock footage of a different item, no filters that change the colour, no editing out flaws.
  • No faces, no personal details. Keep your face, reflections in mirrors, house numbers, post, pets, family photos and number plates out of shot. Hands are fine.
  • Say only what is true. A video is part of your listing. If you would not write it in the description, do not say it in the video.

TikTok Shop UK: claims to avoid

TikTok Shop UK's own policies say claims in e-commerce content must be genuine, accurate and verifiable, and that products must not claim or imply they can cure, heal, treat, prevent or relieve any disease or medical condition. This applies to titles, descriptions, images and videos. Product titles must not include promotional wording (for example "x% off"), your shop URL or seller name, references to TikTok or other marketplaces, or symbols and special characters.

In practice, keep these out of your TikTok Shop copy and videos:

  • Health or medical wording: "cures", "heals", "relieves pain", "treats", "anti-inflammatory", "detox", "boosts immunity", "clinically proven" (unless you hold the evidence and the claim is allowed in that category).
  • Before and after results you cannot prove.
  • "Best", "number one", "better than [brand]" comparisons.
  • Fake urgency: "only 2 left" when that is not true, countdowns that reset, "price going up tomorrow" when it is not.
  • "Guaranteed", "100% safe", "non-toxic", "eco-friendly" or "sustainable" unless you can back it up with specific, checkable facts.
  • Other platform names, discount codes for other sites, or asking buyers to pay you elsewhere.

Rules change. Read TikTok Shop UK's current policies in Seller Center (the Academy pages on product listing, content and prohibited or restricted products) before you list, and check the current rule in the platform's help pages when in doubt.

V1 Faceless product video script (15 to 30 seconds)

Use it when: you want a short, honest video of one item without showing your face or using your own voice.

Paste this:

You are helping a UK seller make a short faceless product video for an item they are selling. Write in UK English.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF]

Platform the video is for: [TIKTOK / INSTAGRAM / TIKTOK SHOP / OTHER]
Length: [15 / 20 / 30] seconds
Voice: [TEXT-TO-SPEECH VOICEOVER / ON-SCREEN TEXT ONLY]

Write a video script as a table with these columns: Seconds, What we see (hands-only or item-only shot), On-screen text (maximum 8 words), Voiceover line (if any).

Rules:
- Only use facts from the Listing Brief. If something I would need is missing, write [CHECK: what is missing] instead of guessing.
- No faces, no people, no reflections. Shots must be possible with a phone, a plain background and my hands.
- Show the flaws listed in the brief on screen, clearly, in at least one shot.
- No hype words (amazing, stunning, must-have, jaw-dropping), no "best", no invented comparisons, no health or medical claims, no fake urgency.
- Open with a plain hook in the first 2 seconds that says what the item is.
- End with a calm call to action that fits the platform (for example "Link in the listing" or "Details in the description"). Do not mention other platforms or ask buyers to pay outside the platform.
- After the table, give me a one-line caption and a list of any [CHECK: ...] items.

V2 Hands-only shot list and showcase ideas

Use it when: you know what the item is but not how to film it without a face or a model.

Paste this:

You are a UK product videographer who only films hands and products, never faces. Write in UK English.

Here is my Listing Brief:
[PASTE YOUR LISTING BRIEF]

My kit: [PHONE ONLY / PHONE AND TRIPOD / PHONE, TRIPOD AND RING LIGHT]
Where I can film: [E.G. KITCHEN TABLE BY A WINDOW, WHITE BEDSHEET, BLANK WALL]

Give me 8 short shot ideas I can film in under 20 minutes. For each shot give: shot name, how to set it up (one or two lines), what it proves to the buyer (size, texture, how it works, condition), and roughly how many seconds to film.

Rules:
- No faces, no people wearing the item from the neck up, no mirrors that could show me. Hands, flat lays, item on a surface, or item on a plain hanger or mannequin only.
- Include at least one shot that shows scale (next to a common object or tape measure) and at least one clear flaw shot if the brief lists flaws.
- Only use facts from the brief. Where a shot depends on something not in the brief (for example the item lights up), write [CHECK: ...].
- Keep the colour true: tell me to use daylight or one consistent light and no colour filters.
- No props that could be mistaken as included with the item unless the brief says they are included.

What good output looks like:

Invented example: small-brand beech wood phone stand, adjustable angle, fits phones up to 7 inch.

  1. Hero turn. Stand on a white sheet, slowly rotate it by hand. Proves shape and finish. 4 seconds.
  2. Angle adjust. Hand tilts the stand through its angles. Proves it adjusts. 4 seconds.
  3. Phone drop-in. Hand places a phone on the stand, portrait then landscape. Proves fit and use. 5 seconds.
  4. Scale shot. Stand next to a mug. Proves size. 3 seconds.
  5. Grain close-up. Slow pan across the wood in window light. Proves material. 3 seconds.
  6. Base grip. Flip it to show the base pads. Proves it will not slide [CHECK: are there non-slip pads?]. 3 seconds.
  7. Cable gap. Plug a charging cable through the gap. Proves charging while in use [CHECK: is there a cable gap?]. 4 seconds.
  8. What is in the box. Items laid out in a row. Proves contents. 3 seconds.

Note: do not show a phone brand logo prominently, and make clear the phone is not included.

Check before you post:

  • Does any prop (phone, cable, mug) look like it comes with the item? Say clearly what is not included.
  • Is the colour on your screen the same as the real item in daylight?
  • Have you answered every [CHECK: ...] before you film shots 6 and 7?
